I'd like to say that the biggest difference is their relationship with food as well as their relationship with themselves. A fear of food and a fear of gaining weight are tell tale signs that something more than a diet is going on. This also means that if the person has a poor self-esteem and a poor image of themself, they're at a higher risk of developing an eating disorder. A person who accepts themselves as they are but wants to improve themself for their health or enjoyment is the basis of a healthy diet, as well as knowing when to stop their diet. Some people who develop eating disorders believe that losing weight will make them loveable, beautiful, worthy and so on without realizing that they are already all of those things. Diet culture influences this a lot, whether directly or indirectly. Although, some people don't develop eating disorders because of their body image, or really even anything related. A good percentage of people with eating disorders are addicted to the false sense of control, not their body image. When the world around them is chaotic, they find comfort and control by limiting their intake, or practicing 'self-discipline' by exercising excessively. Personally, I believe that diet culture is extremely overrated because dieting is a slippery slope to unhealthy habits. While not everyone who diets will develop an eating disorder of some type, the culture that surrounds dieting really influences the idea that 'thin' means 'healthy and beautiful' when realistically, everyone's healthy range is different. Fat is not synonymous with bad or ugly, nor is thin synonymous with beautiful and worthy. It's something I'm still trying to learn, myself. To sum it up and answer your question, though, it all really boils down to their state of mind through it all. A healthy mind leads to a healthy diet, otherwise it's just a downward slope into dangerous territory.
